newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Thousands said dying in Zaire, U.N. council meets.
newsitem.headline: Thousands said dying in Zaire, U.N. council meets.

text.p: Thousands of refugees were reported dead or dying in eastern Zaire on Friday as the U.N. Security Council discussed terms for a multinational force to halt "genocide by starvation".
Nearly every aid organisation of note thundered ever louder warnings as the conflict entered a fourth week with forces on both sides fighting for territory near the eastern city of Goma.

A Reuters correspondent in Goma, seized by rebels a week ago, saw a mortar bomb explode on the outskirts, fired from the direction of Mugunga, a vast refugee camp controlled by armed Rwandan Hutu exiles.
Zaireans in Goma said they were scared the Hutus, who had fought alongside Zairean soldiers, might try to launch a counter-attack to recapture the hungry city of 200,000 people.
Sporadic mortar, anti-aircraft and small-arms fire also boomed and crackled on the edges of the largely looted city.
In New York, Security Council members were due for a second closed-door session later on Friday to complete a text aimed at setting conditions for aid to reach more than a million refugees.
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali pressed in the morning for swift action on the resolution, drafted mainly by France.
Referring to mass killings in Rwanda in 1994, when up to a million people were butchered, he said: "Two years ago we have been confronted by a genocide by the Hutus against the Tutsis."

"Now we are confronted by a new genocide -- I will call it a genocide by starvation, because they are dying, because they are not able to receive food, nor medicaments nor clean water. So we must act, and we must act immediately," he added.

Rwanda, however, told U.N. Special Envoy Raymond Chretien it opposed any army contingent from France, the main advocate for military intervention to help 1.2 refugees and tens of thousands of Zaireans fleeing revolt against President Mobutu Sese Seko.

"France and even Rwanda should abstain from sending troops. The force must be neutral and countries with interests must not participate in the operation," Rwandan President Pasteur Bizimungu told a news conference in Kigali.
Zaire later stated it would no longer allow Rwandan and Burundian refugees in camps on its soil, as a U.N. Special Envoy Raymond Chretien arrived in Kinshasa for talks on their fate.
"No new refugee camps can be built anywhere in Zaire," Information Minister Boguo Makeli said, reading cabinet decisions. Many camps have been abandoned because of fighting.
The U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) warned of mass death in the next three weeks without humanitarian aid corridors.
"People are already starving to death and we estimate that by the end of the month over 80,000 children under three will die," Catherine Bertini, WFP's executive director told Reuters.
Bernard Pecoul, head of Medecins sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Borders), estimated in Paris more than 13,600 refugees died in the last three weeks, not including victims of fighting.

Hutu refugees, desperate Zaireans and demoralised soldiers in Zaire's ragged army are roaming the east region. Some have staggered on swollen legs into Kisangani, up to 500 km (310 miles) from the war zone, Reuters correspondent Matthew Tostevin reported from the Zairean town.
"About 150 km (90 miles) from Goma people started to die, others were too tired to go any further and we left them by the road," said Jean-Paul Masimana, a 20-year-old student..

A Spanish aid worker who escaped to Uganda this week said 175,000 Rwandan refugees who fled Kahindo camp north of Goma after attacks by rebels had headed west on foot through wide volcanic lava fields, which emit dangerous gases.
"They were dying in their thousands. It was an apocalypse," said Fernando Rodriguez, quoting radio distress reports he heard from Zairean colleagues who fled along with the refugees.

In Burundi, WFP official Jean-Luc Siblot said he and other aid workers found on Friday 20,000 Burundian Hutu refugees who had returned to the troubled northwestern province of Cibitoke with little water and food from Zaire.
Food riots hit Goma on Friday with rebels firing into the air to repel more than 1,000 people outside a U.N. warehouse. An emergency health committee in Goma appealed for medicine and equipment.
A Spanish government spokesman in Madrid said the extent of the disaster meant international action was inevitable: "But it will be too late anyhow."
